question.prompt: How many distinct ordered triples \((x,y,z)\) satisfy the equations \[ \begin{aligned} x+2y+4z&=12,\\ xy+4yz+2xz&=22,\\ xyz&=6? \end{aligned} \]

solutions.explanation:
The coefficients in the first equation suggest setting
\[
X=x,\qquad Y=2y,\qquad Z=4z.
\]
This also makes the other equations symmetric: \(XY+YZ+ZX\) is twice the original second left side, and \(XYZ=8xyz\). Thus
\[
X+Y+Z=12,\qquad XY+YZ+ZX=44,\qquad XYZ=48.
\]
These three expressions determine the coefficients of a polynomial whose roots are \(X,Y,Z\). Indeed, multiplying gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(t-X)(t-Y)(t-Z)
&=t^3-(X+Y+Z)t^2\\
&\quad +(XY+YZ+ZX)t-XYZ\\
&=t^3-12t^2+44t-48.
\end{aligned}
\]
To factor this cubic, testing \(t=2\) gives zero, so \(t-2\) is a factor. Division and then quadratic factorization give
\[
\begin{aligned}
t^3-12t^2+44t-48
&=(t-2)(t^2-10t+24)\\
&=(t-2)(t-4)(t-6).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore \(X,Y,Z\) must be \(2,4,6\), each appearing once. In particular, each of the three distinct numbers \(2,4,6\) makes \((t-X)(t-Y)(t-Z)\) zero, so each must equal one of its three listed roots.

Conversely, every ordering of \(2,4,6\) has sum \(12\), pairwise-product sum \(44\), and product \(48\), so every such ordering satisfies the transformed equations. There are \(3\) choices for \(X\), then \(2\) for \(Y\), and \(1\) for \(Z\), giving
\[
3\cdot2\cdot1=6.
\]
The inverse substitution \(x=X\), \(y=Y/2\), \(z=Z/4\) is unique and reverses every transformation, so these orderings give all original solutions without duplication. The answer is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Rescale the variables and recover them as roots
